heading: What each service language can use in the browser
body:
A service in Rust, Go, C#, Kotlin, Dart or Ruby runs in the page, but it does not call the browser itself. It reaches the browser only through Tachyon: the view reads its fields and calls its methods, events carry values in and out, and the storage annotations keep its data. Tachyon also gives every language a small set of browser APIs: `Clock`, `SecureRandom`, `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences`, `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation` (see the next sections). Other browser work, such as a request to the server, lives in a JavaScript or TypeScript service. That service publishes a typed event, and the service in the other language receives it with `OnEvent`.

The table shows what each language can use in the page. Tachyon's tests check every row.

| What | Rust | Go | C# | Kotlin | Dart | Ruby |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Fields and methods for the view | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `publishEvent` and `OnEvent` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Store` and caches | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `LocalState` and `SessionState` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `HTTPClient` | No | No | No | No | No | No |
| `StreamRequest` and `SocketRequest` | No | No | No | No | No | No |
| `Clock` and `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Connectivity`, `PageVisibility`, `Preferences` and their change events | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| `Clipboard`, `Share`, `Notifications` and `Geolocation`, after a grant | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| The current time from the language itself | No, use `Clock` | Yes | Yes | Yes, `System.currentTimeMillis()` | Yes | Yes |
| Random numbers from the language itself | No, use `SecureRandom` | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |
| Wait (sleep) | No | Yes, the page waits | Yes, the page waits | Yes, `Thread.sleep` makes the page wait | Yes, in an `async` method | No |
| Console output | No | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes | Yes |

Send requests from a JavaScript or TypeScript client. Its answers, and the messages of a stream or a socket, reach the other languages as typed events. In Rust, `std::time::SystemTime::now()` and `std::thread::sleep` stop the service with an error, and `println!` prints nothing. Use Tachyon's `Clock` and `SecureRandom` instead (see "Clock and secure random numbers"). Ruby refuses `sleep`, because a Ruby call must return before the page goes on.

Tachyon refuses code that calls the browser directly, and the build stops with `TY1317`: Go `syscall/js`; Dart `dart:js_interop`, `dart:js`, `dart:js_util`, `dart:html`, `package:web` and `package:js`; C# `System.Runtime.InteropServices.JavaScript`, `JSImport`, `JSExport` and `JSHost`; Rust `wasm_bindgen`, `web_sys`, `js_sys` and `wasm_import_module`; Kotlin `external`, `@JsFun`, `@JsExport`, `@JsModule`, `@JsName`, `js(…)`, `kotlinx.browser`, `org.w3c` and `kotlin.js`; and Ruby `TachyonWeb` and `JS`. Such code breaks the test units of the language, and a native target has no browser. Tachyon's own code on the page is not checked.

In the example, `PlaceService` in JavaScript reads the browser and publishes a `PlaceFound` event. `MapService` in Rust or Go receives the event with `OnEvent`. The same pattern works for any browser API outside Tachyon's set.
